subject: Accounting
title: What Is Cost Accounting?
description: A short lesson to help you apply What Is Cost Accounting?.

hook.text: A pizza shop charges $12 per pizza. Does anyone know what each pizza actually costs to make?

buildup.text: Cost accounting tracks the money spent on producing goods or delivering services.

discovery.text: It breaks costs into ingredients, labor, rent, utilities, and overhead—revealing the true cost per unit.

twist.text: Many businesses set prices by gut feeling. Cost accounting replaces guessing with data.

climax.text: Without it, a company might sell products for less than they cost—and slowly go bankrupt.

punchline.text: You can't price right if you don't know your costs.

quiz.question: What does cost accounting track?
options: The cost of producing goods or services

details.summary: Cost accounting is the branch of accounting that captures, classifies, and analyzes the costs of producing goods and services. This topic introduces cost accounting's purpose, how it differs from financial accounting, and its role in management decision-making.
details.whyItMatters: Financial accounting tells you total profit; cost accounting tells you which products, services, and activities generate that profit—and which destroy it. Without cost accounting, managers are flying blind.
takeaways: Cost accounting focuses on internal decision-making rather than external financial reporting
It provides the data for pricing, budgeting, product-mix decisions, and efficiency improvements
Unlike financial accounting, cost accounting has no required standards—companies design systems to fit their needs

faq.question: What is cost accounting?
faq.answer: Cost accounting is the process of recording, classifying, and analyzing all costs associated with producing a product or delivering a service. It provides managers with detailed cost information for pricing, budgeting, cost control, and strategic decisions.

faq.question: How is cost accounting different from financial accounting?
faq.answer: Cost accounting focuses on internal decision-making — tracking, analyzing, and allocating costs to products, services, and departments. Financial accounting reports to external stakeholders. Cost accounting provides granular data managers need for pricing and budgeting.
